title: Correlated Departmental Average Comparison
description_markdown: Find all employees who earn more than the average salary of their own department using a correlated subquery. Return `e.first_name`, `e.salary`, and `e.dept_id`. Exclude NULL `dept_id`. Order by `e.dept_id` ASC, `e.salary` DESC.
starter_query:
-- Correlated subquery
SELECT e.first_name, e.salary, e.dept_id
FROM employees e
WHERE e.salary > (SELECT AVG(e2.salary) FROM employees e2 WHERE ...)
solution_query: SELECT e.first_name, e.salary, e.dept_id FROM employees e WHERE e.dept_id IS NOT NULL AND e.salary > (SELECT AVG(e2.salary) FROM employees e2 WHERE e2.dept_id = e.dept_id) ORDER BY e.dept_id ASC, e.salary DESC, e.emp_id ASC;
solution_explanation: The inner query references `e.dept_id` from the outer query, evaluating departmental averages per row.
hints: Focus on the required WHERE, JOIN, or GROUP BY clause conditions.

Query: SELECT e.first_name, e.salary, e.dept_id FROM employees e WHERE e.dept_id IS NOT NULL AND e.salary > (SELECT AVG(e2.salary) FROM employees e2 WHERE e2.dept_id = e.dept_id) ORDER BY e.dept_id ASC, e.salary DESC, e.emp_id ASC;

-- Correlated subquery comparing employee to manager

title: Calculate Customer Lifetime Spend via Correlated Subquery
description_markdown: Calculate each customer's lifetime total spending on completed orders (`order_status = 'completed'`) using a correlated subquery in the SELECT list. Wrap the subquery with `COALESCE(..., 0.00)` to handle customers with no completed purchases as `lifetime_spend`. Return `c.customer_id`, `c.first_name`, and `lifetime_spend`. Order by `c.customer_id` ascending.
starter_query:
-- Correlated subquery for lifetime spend
SELECT c.customer_id, c.first_name,
       COALESCE((SELECT SUM(o.total_amount) FROM orders o WHERE ...), 0.00) AS lifetime_spend
FROM customers c
ORDER BY c.customer_id ASC;
solution_query: SELECT c.customer_id, c.first_name, COALESCE((SELECT SUM(o.total_amount) FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.customer_id AND o.order_status = 'completed'), 0.00) AS lifetime_spend FROM customers c ORDER BY c.customer_id ASC;
solution_explanation: The correlated subquery sums completed orders per customer; COALESCE converts NULL sums into 0.00.
common_mistakes: Forgetting the filter o.order_status = 'completed'.
interview_tip: Always consider COALESCE when aggregating nullable sets in correlated scalar subqueries.
hints: Query: SELECT c.customer_id, c.first_name, COALESCE((SELECT SUM(o.total_amount) FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.customer_id AND o.order_status = 'completed'), 0.00) AS lifetime_spend FROM customers c ORDER BY c.customer_id ASC;

title: Calculate Product Average Review Rating in SELECT
description_markdown: For each product, project its average customer review rating rounded to 2 decimal places (`ROUND(AVG(r.rating), 2) AS avg_rating`) using a correlated subquery in the SELECT list. Filter out products that have no reviews (where `avg_rating IS NOT NULL` in the main query or via `WHERE (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM reviews r2 WHERE r2.product_id = p.product_id) > 0`). Return `product_id`, `product_name`, and `avg_rating`. Order by `product_id` ascending.
starter_query:
-- Correlated subquery for average product rating
SELECT p.product_id, p.product_name,
       (SELECT ROUND(AVG(r.rating), 2) FROM reviews r WHERE r.product_id = p.product_id) AS avg_rating
FROM products p
WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM reviews r2 WHERE r2.product_id = p.product_id)
ORDER BY p.product_id ASC;
solution_query: SELECT p.product_id, p.product_name, (SELECT ROUND(AVG(r.rating), 2) FROM reviews r WHERE r.product_id = p.product_id) AS avg_rating FROM products p WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM reviews r2 WHERE r2.product_id = p.product_id) ORDER BY p.product_id ASC;
solution_explanation: Computes average rating for reviewed products using a correlated subquery and filters out unreviewed items using EXISTS.
common_mistakes: Omitting the ROUND function to 2 decimal places.
interview_tip: Combining a SELECT scalar subquery with an EXISTS filter in WHERE guarantees non-null scalar metrics.
hints: Use `EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM reviews r2 WHERE r2.product_id = p.product_id)`.

Query: SELECT p.product_id, p.product_name, (SELECT ROUND(AVG(r.rating), 2) FROM reviews r WHERE r.product_id = p.product_id) AS avg_rating FROM products p WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM reviews r2 WHERE r2.product_id = p.product_id) ORDER BY p.product_id ASC;

title: Identify Employees Earning Below Departmental Mean
description_markdown: Use a correlated subquery to find all employees who earn strictly less than the average salary of their own department (`e.salary < (SELECT AVG(e2.salary) FROM employees e2 WHERE e2.dept_id = e.dept_id)`). Exclude employees with NULL `dept_id`. Return `e.emp_id`, `e.first_name`, `e.dept_id`, and `e.salary`. Order by `e.dept_id` ASC, `e.salary` ASC, `e.emp_id` ASC.
starter_query:
-- Correlated subquery for below department average
SELECT e.emp_id, e.first_name, e.dept_id, e.salary
FROM employees e
WHERE e.dept_id IS NOT NULL
  AND e.salary < (SELECT ...)
ORDER BY e.dept_id ASC, e.salary ASC, e.emp_id ASC;
solution_query: SELECT e.emp_id, e.first_name, e.dept_id, e.salary FROM employees e WHERE e.dept_id IS NOT NULL AND e.salary < (SELECT AVG(e2.salary) FROM employees e2 WHERE e2.dept_id = e.dept_id) ORDER BY e.dept_id ASC, e.salary ASC, e.emp_id ASC;

title: Orders Exceeding Customer's Remaining Orders Average
description_markdown: Using a correlated subquery, find orders whose `total_amount` is strictly greater than the average `total_amount` of all other orders placed by the same customer (`o2.customer_id = o.customer_id AND o2.order_id != o.order_id`). Only include orders where the customer has at least one other order (`EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o3 WHERE o3.customer_id = o.customer_id AND o3.order_id != o.order_id)`). Return `order_id`, `customer_id`, and `total_amount`. Order by `customer_id` ASC, `order_id` ASC.
starter_query:
-- Correlated subquery excluding current row
SELECT o.order_id, o.customer_id, o.total_amount
FROM orders o
WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o3 WHERE o3.customer_id = o.customer_id AND o3.order_id != o.order_id)
  AND o.total_amount > (SELECT AVG(o2.total_amount) FROM orders o2 WHERE o2.customer_id = o.customer_id AND o2.order_id != o.order_id)
ORDER BY o.customer_id ASC, o.order_id ASC;
solution_query: SELECT o.order_id, o.customer_id, o.total_amount FROM orders o WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o3 WHERE o3.customer_id = o.customer_id AND o3.order_id != o.order_id) AND o.total_amount > (SELECT AVG(o2.total_amount) FROM orders o2 WHERE o2.customer_id = o.customer_id AND o2.order_id != o.order_id) ORDER BY o.customer_id ASC, o.order_id ASC;
solution_explanation: Excludes the current order row from the calculated benchmark to see if this particular order is an outlier compared to the rest of the customer's history.
common_mistakes: Including the current order in the benchmark average, which drags the average up.
interview_tip: Leave-one-out metrics are a hallmark of anomaly detection algorithms in SQL.
hints: Exclude the current order in the subquery using `o2.order_id != o.order_id`.
Check `EXISTS` to ensure other orders exist for that customer.

Query: SELECT o.order_id, o.customer_id, o.total_amount FROM orders o WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o3 WHERE o3.customer_id = o.customer_id AND o3.order_id != o.order_id) AND o.total_amount > (SELECT AVG(o2.total_amount) FROM orders o2 WHERE o2.customer_id = o.customer_id AND o2.order_id != o.order_id) ORDER BY o.customer_id ASC, o.order_id ASC;
